newsitem.title: USA: Clinton Cabinet nominees hailed in Senate.
newsitem.headline: Clinton Cabinet nominees hailed in Senate.

text.p: President Bill Clinton's choice of personnel for his new national security team won praise in the Senate on Thursday but Republicans coupled their compliments with a swipe at Clinton's policies.

Senators of both parties predicted that the nominees -- U.N. Ambassador Madeleine Albright as secretary of state, Republican Sen. William Cohen as defence secretary and National Security Adviser Anthony Lake as CIA director -- will win easy Senate confirmation.
Samuel Berger, picked by Clinton to succeed Lake, does not require Senate confirmation.
"Ambassador Albright's historic nomination recognises the potential contribution her energy and ability can bring to American diplomacy," Republican Leader Trent Lott said in a statement.
"As secretary of state she will have an opportunity to rethink her strategy of 'assertive multilateralism' to ensure the U.S. -- not the U.N. -- is in the driver's seat."
Similar comments were made by other Republicans who have long been critical of Clinton's foreign policies.

Senate Foreign Relations Committee Chairman Jesse Helms, R-North Carolina, called Albright "a tough and courageous lady" but noted he had not agreed with all her positions and Texas Republican Kay Bailey Hutchison, while praising Albright, criticised U.S. "deferral" to the United Nations in operations in Somalia and Bosnia.
Hutchison said she hoped Cohen would be help reverse "the administrtation's drift and indecision."
The choice of Cohen, a senior member of the Armed Services Committee with a reputation as a strategic thinker, as defence secretary was hailed by both Republicans and Democrats.

Naming a Republican was seen as an astute move by Clinton as he prepares to deal with a Republican Congress in his second term. Cohen "has won widespread respect for his ability to forge bipartisan consensus on national security issues during his 18 years in the U.S. Senate," Sen. Joseph Biden, D-Delaware, said.

Sen. John McCain, R-Arizona, Cohen's colleague on the Armed Services Committee, said he expected Cohen to spend most of his time on policy issues and would need capable managerial help to run day-to-day business at the vast, complex Pentagon.
Hearings on the nominations are expected early next year and will provide a forum for an intense Senate examination of Clinton foreign policies.
Sen. Arlen Specter, R-Pennsylvania, chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee, praised Lake's nomination as CIA chief, calling him "very able."
Specter indicated he would look into Lake's role in the administration's former policy of tacit acquiescence to Iranian arms sales to Bosnian Moslems, an issue that Specter has pursued.
He called Cohen "terrific," adding: "He's not a yes man, and you need someone like that in the Cabinet."
